en.title: United States: continental scale, federal fragmentation and the institutions behind dollar-centered power
en.deck: A structural dossier on how federal institutions, regional production, demographics and capital markets shape U.S. capacity and the global transmission of dollar conditions.
en.regime: Structural context: concentrated national monetary and financial power coexists with decentralized physical implementation and regionally uneven productive constraints.
en.key_risk: Treating national financial power as equivalent to frictionless domestic implementation obscures housing, infrastructure, labor and industrial bottlenecks.

selection_rationale: The United States is materially implicated by the Federal Reserve structural assessment and the September 25 global-macro transmission mechanism. Existing public research explains the Fed and daily market conditions but does not supply reusable country-level context linking federalism, regional production, demographics, infrastructure and dollar-centered financial power.
contrary_evidence: Deep capital markets, energy production, research capacity and a continental domestic market argue against a simple structural-decline thesis.
Below-average industrial utilization, uneven infrastructure constraints and import dependence in selected supply chains argue against a frictionless-dominance thesis.
limitations: Current statistics are point-in-time and must be revalidated in future event-driven research.
A country-level dossier cannot resolve large state and metropolitan differences; those should be treated separately when material.
